'''Neil Gunther''' (born 15 August 1950) is a [[computer]] [[information system]]s [[research]]er best known internationally for developing the [[open-source license|open-source]] [[performance modeling]] software [https://www.perfdynamics.com/Tools/PDQ.html Pretty Damn Quick (PDQ)] along with the [http://www.perfdynamics.com/iBook/gcap.html Guerrilla approach] to computer capacity planning and performance analysis. He has also been cited for his contributions to the theory of large [[Transient (computer programming)|transients]] in [[computer systems]] and [[packet network]]s, and his [http://www.perfdynamics.com/Manifesto/USLscalability.pdf  universal law of computational scalability].<ref>Microsoft developer blog comparing
[http://blogs.msdn.com/ddperf/archive/2009/04/29/parallel-scalability-isn-t-child-s-play-part-2-amdahl-s-law-vs-gunther-s-law.aspx#9576239 Amdahl's law with Gunther's law] (2009)</ref><ref>Computer Measurement Group [http://cmg.org/measureit/issues/mit58/m_58_8.html Interview part 1] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110722152531/http://cmg.org/measureit/issues/mit58/m_58_8.html |date=22 July 2011 }} [http://www.cmg.org/measureit/issues/mit59/m_59_16.html  and part 2] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130520185539/http://cmg.org/measureit/issues/mit58/m_58_8.html |date=20 May 2013 }}  (2009)</ref><ref>Springer [https://www.springer.com/computer/communications/book/978-3-540-26138-4?detailsPage=aboutTheAuthor author biography]</ref><ref>Oracle [http://www.hotsos.com/sym_speakers_gunther.html performance experts]</ref><ref>La Trobe University [http://www.latrobe.edu.au/alumni/profiles/full-profile?queries_name_query=Gunther&search_page_22160_submit_button=Submit&current_result_page=0&results_per_page=0&submitted_search_category=&mode=results alumnus profile] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607095311/http://www.latrobe.edu.au/alumni/profiles/full-profile?queries_name_query=Gunther&search_page_22160_submit_button=Submit&current_result_page=0&results_per_page=0&submitted_search_category=&mode=results |date=7 June 2011 }}</ref><ref>[http://www.neilgunther.com/jcdnjg.pdf Interview] with [[John C. Dvorak]] (1998)</ref>

Gunther is a Senior Member of both the [[Association for Computing Machinery]] (ACM) and the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]] (IEEE), as well as a member of the [[American Mathematical Society]] (AMS), [[American Physical Society]] (APS), [[Computer Measurement Group]] (CMG) and ACM [[SIGMETRICS]].{{fact|date=July 2026}}

== Education ==
Gunther is an Australian of German and Scots ancestry, born in [[Melbourne]] on 15 August 1950. He grew up in the suburb of [[North Balwyn]], matriculating from [[Balwyn High School]] in 1968.

He obtained a B.Sc in Chemistry in 1971, as well as a B.Sc.(Hons) in Physics, under Dr. Tomas M. Kalotas in 1974, and an M.Sc. in Applied Mathematics, under Prof. [[Christie Jayaratnam Eliezer|Christie J. Eliezer]]) in 1976; all from [[LaTrobe University]]. He then obtained a Ph.D. in Theoretical Physics from [[Southampton University]] in 1980.

== Research ==
Gunther taught physics at [[San Jose State University]] from 1980 to 1981. He then joined Syncal Corporation as a  scientist contracted by [[NASA]] and [[JPL]] to develop thermoelectric materials for their deep-space missions.  There, he discovered that the stability of the silicon–germanium (Si-Ge) thermoelectric alloy was controlled by a soliton-based precipitation mechanism.<ref name=PhaseTran1>{{cite journal |author = Gunther, N. J., Nicole, D. A., Wallace, D. J. | title=Goldstone Modes in Vacuum Decay and First-order Phase Transitions |journal= Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General |volume=13 |page=1755|year = 1980 | url=https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/251466/1/jav13i5p1755.pdf}}</ref> 
<ref name=SiGe>{{cite journal |author = Gunther, Neil J. | title=Solitons and Their Role in the Degradation of Modified Silicon-Germanium Alloys |journal=Proc. IEEE Fourth Int. Conf. on Thermoelectric Energy Conversion | publisher = IEEE |volume=82CH1763-2 |pages=89–95 | year = 1982 |url =http://www.neilgunther.com/DeepSpace/thermo82.pdf}}</ref> JPL used his work to select the next generation thermoelectric  materials for the [[Galileo (spacecraft)|Galileo mission]] launched in 1989.

In 1982, Gunther joined the [[Xerox PARC]] research center to develop parametric and functional test software for PARC's small-scale [[VLSI]] design fabrication line. Ultimately, he was recruited onto the ''Dragon'' multiprocessor workstation project where he also developed the ''PARCbench'' multiprocessor benchmark.
In 1989, he developed a version of [[Feynman]]'s path integral formalism for analyzing performance degradation in large-scale computer systems and packet networks.<ref name=LrgTrans>{{Cite journal | author = Gunther, Neil J. | title = Path Integral Methods for Computer Performance Analysis | journal = Information Processing Letters | volume = 32 | pages = 7–13 | year = 1989 | url = http://dblp.uni-trier.de/rec/bibtex/journals/ipl/Gunther89| doi = 10.1016/0020-0190(89)90061-6 | url-access = subscription }}</ref>

In 1990 Gunther joined [[Pyramid Technology]] (later absorbed into [[Fujitsu Technology Solutions]] via a merger with [[Fujitsu Siemens Computers]]) where he held positions as senior scientist and manager of the Performance Analysis Group that was responsible for attaining industry-high [[Transaction Processing Performance Council|TPC]] benchmarks on their [[Unix]] multiprocessors. 
The progenitor of the [https://www.perfdynamics.com/Manifesto/USLscalability.pdf Universal Scalability Law], or USL model, was developed to assess and predict in-house TPC benchmark scalability.<ref name=UniScaling>{{cite journal | author = Gunther, Neil J. | title=A Simple Capacity Model for Massively Parallel Transaction Systems |journal=Proc. CMG Conf. |place=San Diego, California | publisher = Computer Measurement Group |pages=1035–1044 | year = 1993 | url = http://www.perfdynamics.com/Papers/njgCMG93.pdf}}</ref> 
That work was eventually elaborated upon in Chaps. 4-6 of ''the Guerrilla book''<ref name=GCAPbk>{{cite book
|last=Gunther |first=Neil
|title=Guerrilla Capacity Planning
|publisher=Springer
|year=2007}}</ref>  
He also performed event-based queueing simulations for the design of the ''Reliant RM1000'' parallel database server.

In 1994 Gunther founded [https://www.perfdynamics.com  Performance Dynamics Company] as a sole proprietorship, registered in [[California]], to provide consulting and [https://www.perfdynamics.com/Classes/schedule.html educational services] for the management of high performance computer systems with an emphasis on [[Profiling (computer programming)|performance analysis]] and enterprise-wide [[capacity planning]]. 
Training classes based on his [https://www.perfdynamics.com/iBook/gcap.html Guerrilla Capacity Planning] techniques have been presented worldwide at companies like [[Deutsche Bank]], [[FedEx]], [[Vodafone]], and [[Walmart]]. 
He went on to release and develop his own [[open-source license|open-source]] [[Profiling (computer programming)|performance modeling]] [[software]] called "PDQ (Pretty Damn Quick)" around 1998. That software also accompanied his first textbook on performance analysis entitled ''The Practical Performance Analyst''. Several additional books followed. Additionally, the original [https://www.perfdynamics.com/Manifesto/USLscalability.pdf Universal Scalability Law] (USL) was extended in two ways <ref name=USLsims>{{cite journal | author = Holtman, James and Gunther, Neil J.
|title=Getting in the Zone for Successful Scalability
|journal=Proc. CMG Conf. |place=Las Vegas, Nevada | publisher = Computer Measurement Group
|pages=123-136 | year = 2008 | url =
https://arxiv.org/pdf/0809.2541}}</ref>{{ Ordered list | type=i
| A third parameter was introduced that made it easier to solve the USL using nonlinear statistical regression techniques, as well as gain more information about scalability characteristics.
| Discrete-event simulations were used to corroborate the correctness of two earlier [https://www.perfdynamics.com/Manifesto/USLscalability.pdf theorems] (from 2002 and 2008) that had been used to derive the USL from formal queueing theory.}}


From 2005 to 2008, Gunther was a member of the Quantum Engineering team at [[EPFL]] that developed a CMOS-based single-photon array imager (a quantum camera) capable of detecting intensity correlated photons.<ref name=SPAD1>{{cite journal | author = Gunther, Neil J. and Beretta, G. B. | title=Towards Practical Design Rules for Quantum Communications and Quantum Imaging Devices |journal=Proc. Proc. 5893 of Optics & Photonics: Quantum Communications and Quantum Imaging III |place=San Diego, California | publisher = Society of Photo-Optical instrumentation Engineers| year = 2005}}</ref>
<ref name=SPAD2>{{cite journal | author =  Charbon, E.,  Gunther, N. J., Boiko, D. L., Beretta, G. B. | title=Design Rules for Quantum Imaging Devices: Experimental Progress Using CMOS Single-Photon Detectors |journal=Proc. Proc. 5893 of Optics & Photonics: Quantum Communications and Quantum Imaging IV |place=San Diego, California | publisher = Society of Photo-Optical instrumentation Engineers| year = 2005}}</ref>
<ref name=SPAD3>{{cite journal | display-authors=2 |last1=Boiko |first1=D.L. | last2=Gunther | first2=N.J.| last3=Charbon |first3=E | title=A Quantum Imager for Intensity Correlated Photons |journal=New Journal of Physics | volume= 11 | page= 013001| year = 2009}}</ref>

Current research interests include applying the [https://www.perfdynamics.com/Manifesto/USLscalability.pdf Universal Scalability Law] to [[GenAI]] platforms.<ref name=LLMScaling>{{cite journal | author = Gunther, Neil J. | title=Does the Efficient Compute Frontier Represent New Physics? |journal=Proc. APS Global Physics Summit |place=Anaheim, California | publisher = American Physical Society | year = 2025 | url = https://speakerdeck.com/drqz/does-the-efficient-compute-frontier-represent-new-physics}}</ref>
<ref name=LLMScalingQ>{{cite journal | author = Gunther, Neil J. | title=Titan Transients and LLM Scalability: The ghost in the machine |journal=ACM Queue | publisher = Association for Computing Machinery | year = 2026 | url = https://queue.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3819082}}</ref>

== Awards ==
* Senior Member ACM (elected April 2009).
* Senior Member IEEE (elected February 2009).
* Recipient of the [https://web.archive.org/web/20081228120202/http://www.cmg.org/national/michelson-nominations.html A. A. Michelson Award], December 2008.
* Summer Research Institute visitor, [[EPFL]] 2006 and 2007.
* Lecturer, Western Institute of Computer Science, [[Stanford University]], 1997–2000.
* Best paper award, [[Computer Measurement Group|CMG]] conference 1996.
* Visiting Scholar in Materials Science, Stanford University, 1981–1982.
* Science Research Council Studentship, U.K. 1976–1980.
* Commonwealth Postgraduate Scholarship, Australia 1975–1976.
